bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the National Park Service relating to "Glen Canyon National Recreation Area; Motor Vehicles".
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 19.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution nullifies the final rule issued by the National Park Service titled Glen Canyon National Recreation Area; Motor Vehicles and published on January 13, 2025. The rule modified regulations concerning the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, which is located in northern Arizona and southeastern Utah. For example, the rule limited the use of off-road vehicles, such as off-highway vehicles and all-terrain vehicles, in certain areas.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a National Park Service rule published in January 2025 that restricted the use of off-road vehicles—such as all-terrain vehicles and off-highway vehicles—in certain parts of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, which spans northern Arizona and southeastern Utah. If passed, the resolution would nullify those restrictions and prevent the rule from taking effect.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of off-road vehicles, all-terrain vehicles, and off-highway vehicles would be affected by changes to where their products can be legally operated.
Retailers and dealers selling off-road recreational vehicles would see changes in market demand based on access restrictions in this recreation area.
Tourism operators, outfitters, and lodging businesses serving visitors to Glen Canyon for off-road recreation would be affected by changes in vehicle access rules.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would cancel the final rule issued by the National Park Service titled Glen Canyon National Recreation Area; Motor Vehicles and published on January 13, 2025.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who drives. People who visit public land, and people who live beside it.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in driving, and what a car must have. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
